title: India and US Hold High-Level Nuclear Talks in Washington as IAEA Launches Maritime Reactor Initiative
excerpt: Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Ajit Kumar Mohanty met US Energy Secretary Chris Wright to discuss bilateral civil nuclear cooperation, as India joined 27 nations in launching the IAEA's ATLAS initiative for nuclear-powered ships.
body:
• India's Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Ajit Kumar Mohanty met US Energy Secretary Chris Wright in Washington to discuss strengthening bilateral civil nuclear cooperation.
  • India joined 27 other nations in launching the IAEA's ATLAS initiative, which will explore the use of small modular reactors for civilian ships and floating nuclear power plants.
  • The talks come as India targets 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047 after opening the sector to private and foreign investment through the SHANTI Act.
  • Several US nuclear firms including Westinghouse and Holtec International are exploring partnerships in the Indian market.

Top Indian and American officials held discussions in Washington on Wednesday aimed at deepening bilateral civil nuclear cooperation, as India joined a major international initiative to explore nuclear energy for maritime use.

Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Ajit Kumar Mohanty met US Energy Secretary Chris Wright ahead of the ministerial launch of the International Atomic Energy Agency's Atomic Technologies Licensed for Applications at Sea (ATLAS) initiative, which brought together 28 nations to examine using small modular reactors to power civilian ships and floating power plants.

Bilateral Talks Focus on Policy and Partnerships

The discussions between Mohanty and Wright focused on ongoing developments in the bilateral civil nuclear space and policy measures to strengthen cooperation, according to the Department of Atomic Energy.

https://x.com/SachinJain3939/status/2092994080540340655

"The discussions focused on the ongoing developments in bilateral civil nuclear space and policy measures to further strengthen India-US Civil Nuclear Cooperation for mutual benefit of both the sides."

— Department of Atomic Energy, India

The meeting comes at a pivotal moment for India's nuclear ambitions. The country opened its civil nuclear sector to private players earlier this year through the SHANTI Act, which replaced the 1962 Atomic Energy Act and permits up to 49% foreign direct investment in select segments. India has set a target of 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, up from roughly 8.7 GW today — a more than tenfold expansion that would make it one of the world's largest nuclear growth markets.

Several American nuclear firms have expressed interest in the Indian market. Companies including Westinghouse, Holtec International, Centrus Energy, and Curtiss-Wright have engaged with Indian officials on reactor deployment, fuel supply optimization, and local manufacturing partnerships.

ATLAS: Nuclear Power Goes to Sea

The IAEA's ATLAS initiative, launched at a ministerial conference in Washington on August 26-27, represents a new frontier for nuclear energy. The program will support the maritime industry's exploration of small modular reactors (SMRs) for civilian ship propulsion and offshore floating nuclear power plants.

India was among 28 signatory nations, alongside the United States, United Kingdom, France, Japan, South Korea, and others. Mohanty participated in the ministerial-level launch, placing India among nations examining how advanced reactors could be integrated into civilian maritime infrastructure.

"India's long coastline and our large number of offshore islands together with a vast expanding commercial shipping sector present exciting opportunities for deployment of small modular reactors in offshore energy supply and potentially propulsion of civilian vessels."

— Ajit Kumar Mohanty, Chairman, Atomic Energy Commission of India

IAEA Director General Mariano Grossi framed the initiative as an opportunity to shape the future of both the energy and shipping industries, emphasizing the need for global confidence in safety, security, and non-proliferation standards for nuclear technology at sea.

Strategic Context

The US-India civil nuclear relationship has advanced along two parallel tracks in 2026. India's Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam achieved first criticality in April, marking a milestone in indigenous nuclear capability. Meanwhile, NTPC Limited approved a minority equity stake in Chicago-based Clean Core Thorium Energy — only the second American company in nearly two decades to receive US Department of Energy authorization for nuclear technology transfer to India.

The fiscal 2026 US National Defense Authorization Act also named India as a key partner in Washington's nuclear and Indo-Pacific strategies, mandating a joint consultative mechanism under the US-India Strategic Security Dialogue to assess implementation of the 2008 civil nuclear cooperation agreement.

India has also unveiled its Nuclear Energy Mission, targeting at least five indigenous Bharat Small Modular Reactors by 2033, alongside the broader 100 GW goal by 2047.
